hints: Start by sorting labels A-D into inside versus outside the mitochondrion. Which label points to the fluid outside the organelle and which three point to parts of the organelle itself?
Recall the big location rule from the syllabus - only one of the four stages happens outside mitochondria. Think about which stage does not need any mitochondrial enzymes or membranes.
Now split the inside of the mitochondrion. Which letter is the folded membrane where electron carriers sit, and which letter is the fluid-filled centre where the soluble Krebs enzymes sit?
walkthrough:
Read the Micrograph Labels**
Think of the mitochondrion beside you. A is the outer membrane, B is the cytoplasm outside the mitochondrion, C is the inner membrane folded into cristae, and D is the matrix in the centre. Glycolysis uses enzymes free in the cytoplasm, so it cannot be A, C or D.

Place the Matrix Reactions**
Both the link reaction (pyruvate to acetyl CoA) and the Krebs cycle need the soluble enzymes of the matrix, so both occur at D. They release $CO_2$ and reduced NAD and FAD in that fluid compartment.

Place Oxidative Phosphorylation**
Oxidative phosphorylation needs the electron transport chain and ATP synthase, which are built into the inner mitochondrial membrane. That is the cristae at C, where a proton gradient can be set up across the membrane.
Final answer: glycolysis - B; link reaction - D; Krebs cycle - D; oxidative phosphorylation - C.

hints: Focus on the very end of the electron transport chain. What normally receives the electrons and hydrogen ions after they have passed along the carriers?
If that final acceptor is missing, think about whether electrons can keep flowing. What happens to a chain when the last step is blocked?
Link electron flow to proton movement. What normally powers the pumping of $H^+$ into the intermembrane space, and what happens to the gradient if pumping stops?
Finally link the gradient to ATP production and to carriers. How does $H^+$ flow make ATP, and why do NAD and FAD depend on the chain to be recycled?
walkthrough:
Why Oxygen Matters at the End**
In oxidative phosphorylation, electrons from reduced NAD and FAD pass along carriers in the inner membrane and release energy. At the end, oxygen accepts the electrons plus $H^+$ to form water. It is the terminal acceptor that lets the whole flow continue.

Chain Stops Without Oxygen**
In anaerobic conditions there is no acceptor to remove electrons from the last carrier. The carriers stay reduced and cannot accept more electrons, so the whole electron transport chain stops. No energy is released to pump protons.

No Gradient Means No ATP**
Normally energy from electron flow pumps $H^+$ across the inner membrane into the intermembrane space, building a proton/electrochemical gradient. Without pumping, the gradient falls. Without a gradient there is no downhill flow of $H^+$ through ATP synthase, so ADP + Pi cannot be joined to make ATP. Reduced carriers also cannot be oxidised back to NAD and FAD.

Final answer: Oxygen is the final electron acceptor; without it the electron transport chain stops; fewer/no $H^+$ pumped into the intermembrane space so no proton/electrochemical gradient forms; fewer/no $H^+$ flow through ATP synthase so no ATP made; NAD/FAD not regenerated.

hints: Name the enzyme for the last step of lactate fermentation in animal cells. What substrate does it convert and what product does it make?
Look beyond ATP at that step. What important oxidised carrier is remade when pyruvate is reduced, and why is that carrier needed earlier in glycolysis?
Connect the carrier shortage to energy. If glycolysis cannot keep converting triose phosphate to pyruvate, what happens to the small ATP yield made directly in glycolysis?
walkthrough:
Identify the Blocked Step**
The last step of lactate fermentation is pyruvate reduced to lactate, catalysed by lactate dehydrogenase. Inhibiting it means pyruvate accumulates and little or no lactate forms. This step itself does not make ATP.

Loss of NAD Recycling**
The value of that step is regeneration of NAD from reduced NAD. Glycolysis needs a constant supply of NAD to oxidise triose phosphate to pyruvate. Without recycled NAD, that part of glycolysis slows or stops.

Loss of Glycolytic ATP**
Glycolysis makes a small net gain of ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation when triose phosphate goes to pyruvate. If that flow stops because NAD is missing, cancer cells lose the up to 60% of ATP they were getting from lactate fermentation, even when oxygen is present.

Final answer: Enzyme is lactate dehydrogenase; inhibition gives less/no conversion of pyruvate to lactate; so less/no NAD regenerated; so less/no conversion of triose phosphate to pyruvate; so less/no ATP from substrate-level phosphorylation in glycolysis.
